title: Artificial Intelligence
body:
This course is organised around one object, the [[Rational Agent]]: something that perceives
an environment and selects the action expected to score best against a performance measure its
designer wrote down. Every block of the course is a different answer to how that selection is
made, ordered by how much the agent is told in advance.

Search applies when the agent knows the rules and has to work out their consequences. Utility
theory applies when those consequences carry probabilities. Supervised and unsupervised
learning apply when nobody supplied the rules. Reinforcement learning applies when nobody
supplied the answers either, and the agent has to work them out from consequences that arrive
late.

It runs alongside [[MACHINE LEARNING]], which owns learning from data as a subject in itself,
including the neural network stack and the loss and evaluation machinery. This course owns the
agent, and treats learning as one of the things an agent can do.

## Topics

### The agent frame

[[Rational Agent]] defines the object. An agent has sensors that perceive, actuators that act,
an environment it operates in, and a performance measure that scores the outcome. Rational
means choosing the action with the highest expected score given what the agent knows, so a
rational agent can still get a bad outcome, and a lucky guess is still irrational.

The performance measure is written by the designer, and writing it badly is the classic
failure of the whole frame. An agent scored on cleaned dust will dump the dust and clean it
again, which is a rational solution to the problem as written.

Six properties of the environment decide which algorithm is even applicable:

```
observable      can the agent see the whole state, or part of it
deterministic   does an action always produce the same result
episodic        does this decision affect the next one
static          does the world change while the agent is deciding
discrete        finite states and actions, or continuous
single-agent    is anything else choosing against it
```

Each later block of the course is one of those properties being relaxed, which is the
efficient way to remember what each technique is for.

### Search

When the environment is observable, deterministic and static, the agent can work out the
consequences of a plan before acting. The problem becomes a graph, where a state is a vertex
and an action is an edge, and finding a plan means finding a path.

[[Best-First Search]] is a family of algorithms sharing one structure: hold the frontier in a
priority queue, which is a [[Heap]], ordered by an evaluation function $f(n)$. Changing $f$
changes the algorithm:

| $f(n)$ | Algorithm | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| $g(n)$, cost so far | Dijkstra | finds the cheapest path, explores in every direction |
| $h(n)$, estimated cost remaining | greedy best-first | fast, and returns a path with no guarantee it is shortest |
| $g(n) + h(n)$ | [[A* Search]] | finds the cheapest path while aiming at the goal |

A* is the algorithm the block is built on, and the reason it works is that $f$ estimates the
cost of a complete solution passing through a node, so comparing two nodes compares two whole
plans. It returns an optimal path whenever the [[Heuristic]] never overestimates the remaining
cost, which is admissibility. If $h$ overestimated, A* could reject a node on the true best
path because its estimate looked too expensive.

```
straight-line distance to the goal is an admissible heuristic for road navigation:
no road is shorter than the straight line, so the estimate is never too high
```

Consistency is the stronger condition, requiring $h$ to obey the triangle inequality, and it
makes A* expand each node once. With $h = 0$ every node looks equally promising and the
algorithm becomes Dijkstra. In practice memory is what limits it, since the frontier and the
visited set both grow with the number of expanded nodes.

The algorithm is fixed and the heuristic is the design work. [[Heuristic]] carries the
dominance rule, where a larger admissible heuristic expands fewer nodes because it prunes more
aggressively while staying safe, and the standard method for inventing one, which is to solve
a relaxed version of the problem exactly. Removing a constraint from the 8-puzzle, so tiles may
move through each other, gives an easily computed distance that never overestimates the real
one. [[Weighted Graph]] is what gets searched and [[Time Complexity]] is why a heuristic is
needed at all.

### Adversarial search

Relax the single-agent property and half the moves are chosen by somebody trying to make you
lose. [[Game Trees]] in [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] owns this block, holding minimax, the
$O(b^d)$ growth, alpha-beta pruning down to $O(b^{d/2})$ under good move ordering, static
evaluation functions, and the horizon effect.

Minimax alternates between a player maximising the score and one minimising it, computing each
node's value from its children:

```
        MAX                 3        take the largest child
              /                \
        MIN  3                  2     take the smallest child
           /   \              /   \
          3     5            2     9   leaf scores
```

MAX chooses the left branch, because the right branch lets the opponent hold it to 2.
Alpha-beta returns the identical move and reaches it faster, by abandoning a branch as soon as
it is proved worse than one already examined.

Minimax and [[Expected Utility]] handle uncertainty differently because the uncertainty has a
different source. Minimax assumes the worst case, since an opponent is choosing against you.
Utility theory takes the expected case, since a die has no intentions. A game containing both
needs both. [[Nondeterminism]] and [[NP-Complete]] describe the size of the tree being pruned.

### Deciding under uncertainty

Relax the deterministic property and an action leads to several outcomes with probabilities. A
preference ordering ranks outcomes and cannot price a gamble, because ranking says nothing
about whether a 50% chance of $A$ beats a certain $B$. A [[Utility Function]] assigns a number
to each outcome, which is what makes the comparison possible.

[[Expected Utility]] is the decision rule: choose the action maximising
$\sum_s P(s \mid a) U(s)$. The utility scale is arbitrary, so $U$ and $2U + 7$ describe the
same agent, since maximising one maximises the other.

Utility in money is concave, and that concavity is what risk aversion consists of, with no
extra rule added. Taking $U(x) = \sqrt{x}$ on a coin flip between nothing and $100:

```
expected value:   0.5(0)   + 0.5(100)   = 50
expected utility: 0.5(√0)  + 0.5(√100)  = 5
utility of $50 for certain: √50 = 7.07, which is larger than 5
```

The agent prefers $50 in hand to the gamble, and the certain amount matching the gamble's
utility is $25. Nothing was added to the model to produce that preference; it follows from the
shape of the utility function. The same rule accounts for the value of information, which is
worth exactly what it changes about the decision, and for exploration.
[[Probability]], [[Random Variable]], [[Conditional Probability]] and [[Bayes Theorem]] from
[[STATISTICS]] supply the machinery.

### Optimisation with no gradient

[[Genetic Algorithm]] maintains a population of candidate solutions, scores each by fitness,
selects the better ones, recombines them by crossover, and perturbs them by mutation.

```
population -> score by fitness -> select the fittest -> crossover -> mutate -> repeat
```

Crossover is what makes the method evolutionary, since it combines partial solutions from two
parents, and mutation is what escapes a local optimum by producing a candidate no combination
of parents could reach.

[[Gradient Descent]] requires a differentiable objective and walks downhill from one starting
point to the nearest local minimum. A genetic algorithm requires only a fitness number, so it
applies to discrete and black-box problems where adjusting a parameter slightly has no
meaning, such as choosing an ordering or a wiring layout. The choice follows the objective: a
smooth differentiable one goes to gradients, and a combinatorial or opaque one goes to the
genetic algorithm. [[Optimization]] and [[Multivariable Optimization]] cover the calculus side.

### Learning from labelled examples

Relax the assumption that the rules were supplied. [[Supervised Learning]] gives the agent
examples with correct answers attached and asks it to produce a rule. The task is regression
when the target is a number and [[Classification]] when it is a category, and every model runs
the same loop: choose a model family, choose a [[Loss Function]], minimise it, then check the
result on data the model never saw.

The regression and gradient material already exists elsewhere in the vault, with
[[Linear Regression]] in [[STATISTICS]], [[Logistic Regression]] and the [[Sigmoid]] in
[[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]], and the [[Confusion Matrix]] evaluation set in
[[MACHINE LEARNING]]. What this course adds is trees.

A [[Decision Tree]] is the one model a person can read directly. Each internal node tests one
attribute, each branch is an outcome of that test, and each leaf is a prediction. It is built
by choosing, at each node, the attribute that splits the data most usefully, measured by
information gain, which is the drop in [[Entropy]] the split produces.

```
10 emails, 5 spam and 5 not:      entropy = 1.00 bits, maximum uncertainty

split on "contains the word free":
  yes:  4 emails, 4 spam, 0 not   entropy = 0.00   perfectly decided
  no:   6 emails, 1 spam, 5 not   entropy = 0.65

weighted entropy after the split = 0.4(0.00) + 0.6(0.65) = 0.39
information gain = 1.00 - 0.39 = 0.61 bits
```

The attribute with the largest gain becomes the test, and the procedure repeats on each
branch. This is [[Entropy]] doing applied work for the first time in the vault. Grown to full
depth a tree memorises the training data, giving every example its own leaf, which is
overfitting made visible. [[Random Forest]] turns that weakness into the mechanism: build many
trees, each on a random sample of the data and considering a random subset of attributes at
each split, then average their predictions. The randomisation forces the trees to make
different mistakes, and averaging cancels errors that are uncorrelated. The cost is
interpretability, which was the single tree's advantage.

### Learning without labels

[[Unsupervised Learning]] has no labels, so there is no answer to check against, which is the
real difficulty of the block. The algorithms themselves are short. It also covers anomaly detection,
where the classes are extremely imbalanced by definition and an accuracy figure carries no
information.

[[Clustering]] groups points by closeness, and everything depends on what close means, since
distance is a [[Vector Norm]]. Rescaling one feature changes which points are neighbours, so
feature scaling changes the answer, and in high dimensions the distances between all pairs of
points converge, which makes the nearest point close to meaningless.

k-means is the standard algorithm: place $k$ centres, assign every point to its nearest
centre, move each centre to the mean of its assigned points, and repeat until nothing moves.
It converges, and it converges to a local optimum that depends on where the centres started.
It assumes clusters that are roughly spherical and similar in size, and it needs $k$ in
advance, which is normally the quantity being looked for. The elbow and silhouette methods are
heuristics for choosing it. [[Principal Component Analysis]] reduces dimension before any of
this runs, and [[Mean]] and [[Variance]] are what both techniques operate on.

### Learning from consequences

Relax the last assumption. The agent gets no labels and no description of the environment,
only a scalar reward that can arrive long after the action that earned it. Working out which
of forty moves earned the win is the credit assignment problem, and it is what makes this a
field of its own.

[[Reinforcement Learning]] covers the loop, the discounted return where $\gamma$ sets how much
the agent values future reward against immediate reward, value functions as
[[Expected Utility]] with the utilities unknown, and the exploration against exploitation
trade. $\epsilon$-greedy resolves that trade by taking the best known action most of the time
and a random one with probability $\epsilon$, which is the value-of-information argument
applied.

[[Q-Learning]] is the algorithm. It holds a table $Q(s,a)$ estimating the value of taking
action $a$ in state $s$, and updates it after every step:

$$
Q(s,a) \;\leftarrow\; Q(s,a) + \alpha\Big[\,r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)\Big]
$$

The bracket is the temporal-difference error, the gap between what the agent expected and what
it now believes after seeing the reward $r$ and the next state $s'$. The algorithm is
model-free, so it never builds a model of how the world works, and off-policy, because the
update uses $\max_{a'}$ while the behaviour may have been exploratory, which is what lets it
learn the optimal policy while behaving safely. It converges given enough visits to every
state and action pair.

The table becomes impossible beyond small state spaces, since a board game has more states
than atoms available to store them. Approximating $Q$ with a [[Neural Network]] is where this
course's search and learning blocks meet.

Reward functions, fitness functions and performance measures are the same failure repeated in
three places. Each system optimises the sentence that was actually written down.

## Related courses

- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] is the sibling course. It owns learning from data as a subject, in
  [[Neural Network]], [[Back Propagation]], [[CNN]], [[Loss Function]] and
  [[Confusion Matrix]], while this course owns the agent that might use one.
  [[Classification]], [[MNIST]] and [[Entropy]] are shared between them.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] holds [[Game Trees]], which is this course's adversarial search
  block written a session early, along with [[Random Numbers]], [[Simulation]] and its own
  [[Neural Network]] chapter.
- [[STATISTICS]] supplies [[Probability]], [[Random Variable]],
  [[Conditional Probability]], [[Bayes Theorem]], [[Mean]] and [[Variance]].
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] supplies the [[Heap]] holding the frontier, the
  [[Graph]] being searched, and the [[Tree]] a decision tree is.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] owns the graph context around [[Dijkstra's Algorithm]], which
  is A* with $h = 0$, so the two sets of notes describe one algorithm from opposite ends.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] explains why exact answers are unavailable
  through [[NP-Complete]], and sets the ceiling on any agent at all through
  [[Turing Machine]] and [[Undecidability]].
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] supplies the
  [[Principal Component Analysis]] and [[Vector Norm]] that clustering runs on.
- [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] supply the [[Optimization]] and
  [[Multivariable Optimization]] that gradient methods use.
- [[Systems of Logic]] in `Books/` covers the classical AI material this syllabus leaves out,
  including knowledge representation, logical agents and inference. It is logged as a content
  gap.
